passages.t: A stubborn people, told in advance
passages.happening:
God calls on the house of Jacob, the people called by the name of Israel, who swear by the name of the LORD and invoke the God of Israel, ‘but not in truth or righteousness’ (verse 1). They call themselves after the holy city and lean on the God of Israel (verse 2).

‘I foretold the former things long ago’ (verse 3). Suddenly he acted, and they came to pass. ‘For I knew that you are stubborn; your neck is iron and your forehead is bronze’ (verse 4). So he told them beforehand, so that they could not say an idol had done it (verse 5).

Now he announces new things, hidden things they have never heard (verse 6). They are created now, so the people cannot say they knew them already (verse 7). ‘You have never heard; you have never understood; for a long time your ears have not been open’ (verse 8). God knew how deceitful they were; they were called a rebel from birth.
passages.hearers:
Chapter 48 closes the first half of chapters 40 to 55. The chapters before it argued that the LORD alone is God, named Cyrus, and announced the fall of Babylon and its gods. Now the prophet turns back to Israel, and the tone is sharper than anywhere since chapter 40.

The chapter opens with a list of everything that marked a person as belonging to Israel: the name, descent from Judah, oaths sworn by the LORD's name, and a share in Jerusalem, the holy city. To swear by a god's name was to call that god as witness, a basic act of loyalty. The list ends with a sting: none of it was in truth or righteousness.

The iron neck and bronze forehead were familiar pictures of obstinacy, a neck that will not bend and a brow that will not blush. God says he foretold events precisely because the people were stubborn. Prophecy was given not because Israel was reliable, but to leave them no room to thank anyone else.
passages.later: Moses told Israel that God's choice was never a reward: ‘The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples’ (Deuteronomy 7:7). Hebrews warns Christian readers in the same terms: ‘do not harden your hearts’ (Hebrews 3:8).
passages.hard:
If God knew Israel would be stubborn and treacherous, why did he choose them, and why tell them the future at all?

The chapter faces the question directly. God says he announced events beforehand because Israel was stubborn, so that they could never say an idol had done it. His choice of Israel is never presented in Scripture as a reward for goodness (Deuteronomy 7:7-8 and 9:4-6). It rests on his love and his promise to their ancestors.

Some readers ask whether that makes the choice arbitrary, or Israel's failures beside the point. The chapter holds both God's commitment and Israel's responsibility. God will not abandon his people, and their disobedience still has real consequences. The exile happened. The rescue comes through God's faithfulness to his own name. Nothing here is a reason to blame the Jewish people. The New Testament gives the same warning about a hardened heart to the church (Hebrews 3:8).
passages.asks: The people had every outward mark of belonging to God, but not in truth. Ask which marks of faith you rely on that could be worn without truth. And ask whether you would rather God tell you the future, or whether you would credit something else when it came.

passages.t: Refined in the furnace for the sake of God's name
passages.happening:
‘For the sake of My name I will delay My wrath; for the sake of My praise I will restrain it, so that you will not be cut off’ (verse 9). ‘See, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction’ (verse 10). ‘For My own sake, My very own sake, I will act; for how can I let Myself be defamed?’ (verse 11). He will not give his glory to another.

‘Listen to Me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I have called: I am He; I am the first, and I am the last’ (verse 12). His hand founded the earth and spread out the heavens (verse 13).

Which of the idols foretold these things? ‘The LORD’s chosen ally will carry out His desire against Babylon’ (verse 14). God has called him and brought him, and he will succeed (verse 15). God has not spoken in secret (verse 16). Then a new voice speaks: ‘the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Refining came from metalwork. Silver ore was heated in a crucible until the impurities separated and could be skimmed off. Moses had called Egypt an iron furnace from which God brought Israel. Now exile is a furnace too. God says he refined them not as silver, which many interpreters take to mean he did not use the full heat a silversmith would, or nothing would have been left.

The word name appears five times in the chapter. Israel carried God's name carelessly. God guards it jealously, meaning his character as the nations see it. The rescue from Babylon will happen for that reason, not because the exiles deserved it.

The chosen ally of verse 14 is Cyrus, named in 44:28 and 45:1. Verse 16 then changes speaker. Someone sent by the Lord GOD with his Spirit now speaks, probably the prophet himself, or the Servant who comes forward in the next chapter. Readers have heard both.
passages.later: Moses said the LORD ‘brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt’ (Deuteronomy 4:20). The risen Jesus takes the title of verse 12: ‘I am the First and the Last’ (Revelation 1:17). Malachi pictures the LORD as a refiner of silver (Malachi 3:3).
passages.asks: God says he refined his people, but not as silver, so that they would not be cut off. Ask what furnace you have been through and what it burned away. And ask what it means for you that God acts for the sake of his own name, and not because you earned it.

passages.t: If only you had listened, and go out from Babylon
passages.happening:
‘Thus says the LORD your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 17). He is the God who teaches them for their good and directs them in the way they should go.

‘If only you had paid attention to My commandments, your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like waves of the sea’ (verse 18). Their descendants would have been as many as the sand, and their name would never have been cut off (verse 19).

Then the command the whole section has been building toward. “Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans!” (verse 20). They are to declare it with a shout of joy to the ends of the earth: the LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob (verse 20). ‘They did not thirst when He led them through the deserts; He made water flow for them from the rock’ (verse 21).

The chapter ends with a hard line. The LORD says there is no peace for the wicked (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Verse 18 is a lament from God himself. Peace like a river is shalom, well-being in every part of life, flowing without stopping. It is what obedience would have brought.

The command to leave Babylon assumes the time near the end of the exile, around the Persian capture of the city in 539 BC. The decree of Cyrus allowed the exiles to go home, and the first group returned under Sheshbazzar and later Zerubbabel. Not all went. Many Judeans had built lives in Babylonia, as Jeremiah had told them to do, and a large Jewish community stayed there for centuries. Leaving was a real decision.

Verse 21 recalls the exodus, when water came from the rock in the wilderness. The way home from Babylon is a second exodus.

The last verse closes the first half of chapters 40 to 55. The same words close the second half in 57:21.
passages.later: A voice in Revelation takes up the command for the great city: “Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4). Paul reads the rock of the exodus this way: ‘that rock was Christ’ (1 Corinthians 10:4).
passages.asks: God grieves over the peace his people could have had. Ask what peace you have missed by not listening. And ask what Babylon you have settled into that you would find hard to leave, even if God called you out.
